newsitem.title: USA: Citicorp Q2 sparks debate on growth.
newsitem.headline: Citicorp Q2 sparks debate on growth.

text.p: Citicorp's second-quarter earnings Tuesday touched off a debate about whether the company is still a growth story for investors.
While most analysts agreed that the company's U.S. credit card business did poorly in the quarter, analyst George Salem of Gerard Klauer Mattison said "Citicorp is not doing well, period."
Analyst Robert Albertson of Goldman, Sachs & Co said there are signs problems in the U.S. card business are getting fixed, with the deinquency rate down from the first quarter.

Salem noted that net income in Citicorp's consumer businesses, which includes branches, credit cards and the private bank, was down three percent, while net income in the other main business, the global corporate bank, rose five percent.
For the consumer businesses, it was the second consecutive quarter when net income posted a three percent decline.
Citicorp's overall net income was up eight percent to $1.02 billion and a reduction in shares outstanding boosted per-share earnings 13 percent to $2.10 diluted.

Salem said one source of concern is a series of currency devaluations in the Far East. "This has negative connotations for banks," the analyst said, adding that the effects include higher interest rates, which make it more difficult for borrowers, and increased inflation for a country's imports.

A key part of Citicorp's strategy has been to target emerging markets for the introduction of consumer banking services and later add corporate banking services as a country's financial structure matures.
Salem said the issue boils down to a question of "Where's the growth?" He added, "I think this is a turning point for Citicorp. They have a real challenge ahead of them."

In a statement with the earnings, Citicorp chairman and chief executive John Reed said the company is responding with quality initiatives and cost initiatives to the challenge of a competitive environment.
Albertson said "The basic momentum in emerging markets is totally intact." He said a downturn in branch business in Asia has been offset by solid results in Latin America.
Albertson said the bigger issue for Citicorp was "the depth to which the credit card business fell domestically."

But he noted delinquencies in U.S. cards, considered a leading indictor of charge-offs, declined to 1.86 percent of the portfolio at the end of the quarter from 1.98 percent at the end of 1997's first quarter. The delinquency rate was 1.73 percent a year ago.

Citicorp's stock was off 2-7/8 to 125-5/8 in early afternoon while Chase Manhattan Corp, which also reported second-quarter earnings, was up 9/16 to 102-9/16. Albertson said Chase delivered a "positive surprise."
